lead: A column is a member that carries load mainly in compression. Before any steel is chosen, the designer sorts it: by the way its bars are held, by the way it is loaded, and above all by how slender it is. Slenderness depends on two things, the end restraint, which gives the effective length, and the size of the section. A short column fails by crushing of its materials; a slender column also bows sideways, and that bow adds a moment the designer must include.
prereq: You need the limit state of collapse in compression and the stress block (see Stress block parameters for limit state of collapse), and the idea of a moment of resistance from beam design.

blocks.text: Columns are grouped in four independent ways. A designer states all four before starting.

items: By lateral steel. A tied column has longitudinal bars held by closed ties at a pitch along the height. A helically reinforced (spiral) column has a continuous helix that confines the core, so it carries about 5 % more load and fails in a more ductile way. A composite column has a steel section inside the concrete.

By loading. An axially loaded column carries load through its centroid (only the minimum eccentricity applies). A column with uniaxial bending carries load plus moment about one axis. A column with biaxial bending has moments about both axes, as at the corner of a frame.
By shape. Square, rectangular, circular, and L or T shaped columns at wall corners.

By slenderness. Short or slender, set by the slenderness ratios below. A pedestal is a very short compression member whose effective length is not more than three times its least lateral dimension; it may be of plain concrete.

blocks.text: The frame matters too. A braced column belongs to a frame whose sideways movement is held by shear walls, bracing or a lift core. An unbraced column must resist sway by its own bending. The same column is usually short in a braced frame and may be slender in an unbraced one.

The unsupported length l is the clear height between the floor and the underside of the beam (or slab) that holds the column sideways. The length that buckles is the effective length le = K l, where K depends on how much each end can rotate and move. IS 456 Table 28 gives K for ideal end conditions; the recommended design values are a little larger than the theoretical ones because real joints are never fully fixed.

blocks.text: For a column in a real frame, K comes from the stiffness of the beams meeting at each end (the charts in IS 456 Annex E). A braced frame gives K between 0.65 and 1.0; a sway frame gives K above 1.0.

sections.h3: Slenderness ratio, the limit of 12 and the minimum eccentricity

blocks.where: D is the section depth for bending about the major (x) axis and b the width for bending about the minor (y) axis, both in mm; l<sub>ex</sub> and l<sub>ey</sub> are the effective lengths for buckling about those axes, in mm. If either ratio is 12 or more, the column is slender.

blocks.text: Check both axes. The minor axis usually decides, because b is the smaller dimension. IS 456 also caps the unsupported length at 60 times the least lateral dimension, and for a column free at one end at 100b²/D. A slender column is not forbidden; it simply needs an additional moment for the sideways bow (IS 456 clause 39.7):
M<sub>ay</sub> = (P<sub>u</sub> b / 2000) × (l<sub>ey</sub>/b)²,  reduced by k = (P<sub>uz</sub> − P<sub>u</sub>)/(P<sub>uz</sub> − P<sub>b</sub>) ≤ 1
blocks.where: P<sub>u</sub> is the factored axial load; P<sub>uz</sub> = 0.45f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.75f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub> is the pure axial capacity; P<sub>b</sub> is the axial load at the balanced point (concrete crushing and tension steel yielding together). M<sub>ax</sub> is the same expression with D and l<sub>ex</sub>. Work it only about an axis whose ratio is 12 or more.

blocks.text: Even a short column is never loaded exactly through its centroid. IS 456 clause 25.4 therefore requires every column to be designed for a minimum eccentricity about each axis in turn:
e<sub>min</sub> = l/500 + D/30, not less than 20 mm
blocks.where: l is the unsupported length in mm and D is the lateral dimension in the direction of the eccentricity, in mm. The design moment is then at least P<sub>u</sub> × e<sub>min</sub>.

examples.question: A braced tied column has section b × D = 300 mm × 450 mm and unsupported length 3.6 m, effectively pinned at both ends for buckling about either axis. Find the slenderness ratios, classify the column, and find the minimum eccentricity about each axis.
steps: End conditions: pinned at both ends, no sway, so K = 1.0 and l<sub>ex</sub> = l<sub>ey</sub> = 1.0 × 3600 = 3600 mm.
Major axis (bending in the direction of D = 450 mm): l<sub>ex</sub>/D = 3600/450 = 8.0, which is less than 12.

Minor axis (direction of b = 300 mm): ley/b = 3600/300 = 12.0. IS 456 calls a column short only when the ratio is less than 12, so a ratio of exactly 12.0 makes the column slender about the minor axis.
Classification: slender about the minor axis only. The additional moment is needed about y; about x the column behaves as short.
Minimum eccentricity about y (across b): 3600/500 + 300/30 = 7.2 + 10.0 = 17.2 mm, below the 20 mm floor, so e<sub>min,y</sub> = 20.0 mm.
Minimum eccentricity about x (across D): 3600/500 + 450/30 = 7.2 + 15.0 = 22.2 mm, above 20 mm, so e<sub>min,x</sub> = 22.2 mm.
examples.answer: l<sub>ex</sub>/D = 8.0 and l<sub>ey</sub>/b = 12.0: the column is slender about the minor axis (12 is not less than 12). e<sub>min</sub> = 22.2 mm about x and 20.0 mm about y.

examples.question: The same column carries P<sub>u</sub> = 1200 kN and has 6 bars of 16 mm (3 on each 450 mm face), 8 mm ties, 40 mm clear cover, M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. Find the additional moment about the minor axis and its reduced value.
steps: Additional moment: M<sub>ay</sub> = (P<sub>u</sub> b/2000)(l<sub>ey</sub>/b)² = (1200 × 300/2000) × 12.0² = 180 × 144 = 25920 kN·mm = 25.92 kN·m.

Balanced point about y: cover to bar centre d′ = 40 + 8 + 8 = 56 mm, so d = 300 − 56 = 244 mm and x<sub>u,b</sub> = 0.0035/(0.0035 + 0.0038) × 244 = 117.0 mm (0.0038 = 0.87f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub> + 0.002 = 0.0018 + 0.002, the limiting tension strain for Fe415). Concrete force 0.36 × 20 × 450 × 117.0 = 379.0 kN; compression bars (strain 0.00182) add about 188.1 kN; tension bars at 0.87f<sub>y</sub> take 217.7 kN. P<sub>b</sub> = 349.4 kN.

Reduced additional moment: 0.309 × 25.92 = 8.00 kN·m. Compare the minimum-eccentricity moment P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min,y</sub> = 1200 × 0.020 = 24.0 kN·m: the column is designed about y for its first-order moment (at least 24.0 kN·m) plus 8.00 kN·m.
examples.answer: M<sub>ay</sub> = 25.92 kN·m before reduction; with P<sub>uz</sub> = 1580 kN and P<sub>b</sub> = 349 kN, k = 0.31 and the additional moment is 8.0 kN·m.

traps: Calling a ratio of exactly 12 short. IS 456 says short only when both ratios are less than 12.
Checking only the major axis. The minor axis has the smaller dimension and usually the larger ratio.
Using the clear height in place of l<sub>e</sub>, or the theoretical K (0.5) in place of the design K (0.65) for a fixed–fixed column.
Forgetting the 20 mm floor on e<sub>min</sub>, or using D for both axes. Each axis uses its own dimension.
Adding the full additional moment without the factor k. When P<sub>u</sub> is well above P<sub>b</sub>, k cuts M<sub>a</sub> sharply.

quiz.q: Define effective length and give the IS 456 design value of K for a column fixed at both ends with no sway.
quiz.a: Effective length l<sub>e</sub> = K l is the length that buckles, set by the end restraints. For fixed–fixed with no sway, the theoretical K is 0.5 and the design value is 0.65.

quiz.q: Why does IS 456 require a minimum eccentricity even for an axially loaded column?
quiz.a: Columns are never perfectly straight or loaded exactly at the centroid: formwork tolerances, bar positions and beam reactions shift the load. e<sub>min</sub> = l/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm makes the design cover that unavoidable moment.

quiz.q: A braced column of 250 mm × 400 mm is 4.0 m high and fixed at both ends. Classify it.
quiz.a: l<sub>e</sub> = 0.65 × 4000 = 2600 mm. 2600/400 = 6.5 and 2600/250 = 10.4; both are less than 12, so the column is short.

quiz.q: Find e<sub>min</sub> for a 300 mm × 300 mm column of unsupported length 2.4 m.
quiz.a: 2400/500 + 300/30 = 4.8 + 10 = 14.8 mm, below 20 mm, so e<sub>min</sub> = 20 mm about each axis.

quiz.q: A 300 mm × 600 mm column has l<sub>e</sub> = 4.2 m about both axes. A student calls it short because 4200/600 = 7.0. Is the student right?
quiz.a: No. About the minor axis 4200/300 = 14.0, which is 12 or more, so the column is slender about that axis and needs the additional moment M<sub>ay</sub>.

quiz.q: Explain why the same column can be short in a braced frame and slender in a sway frame.
quiz.a: Sway lets the column ends move sideways, so K rises above 1 (for example 1.2 for both ends fixed in rotation). A larger l<sub>e</sub> pushes l<sub>e</sub>/b past 12 even though the section and height are unchanged.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design offices often skip K and run a second-order (P-Δ) analysis in frame software, which puts the sway moments straight into the column forces. Search for "P-delta analysis" and "moment magnification method".
